concepts.name: Canal Irrigation: Perennial vs. Inundation Canals
key_dimensions: Structural difference: perennial canals draw from dammed rivers year-round vs. inundation canals fed only during flood season
Regional distribution: perennial canals dominant in Punjab, Haryana, UP; inundation canals in older deltaic systems like Mahanadi delta
UPSC trap: inundation canals are NOT the same as flood irrigation — they are structured channels
Declining relevance of inundation canals post-dam construction and why they still persist in certain areas

concepts.name: Tank Irrigation: Historical Significance and Decline
key_dimensions: Historical dominance in Peninsular India — Deccan plateau, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka — linked to hard rock terrain limiting groundwater access
Role of ancient rulers (Cholas, Vijayanagara Empire) in tank construction — cultural and civilizational importance
Reasons for decline: siltation, encroachment, neglect of maintenance, shift to bore wells, breakdown of community management (Kudimaramath system)
UPSC trap: tanks are the PRIMARY source of irrigation in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, NOT canals — a commonly confused fact

concepts.name: Well and Tube Well Irrigation: Dominance and Regional Patterns
key_dimensions: Well/tube well irrigation accounts for the LARGEST share of net irrigated area in India (~60%+) — a frequently tested fact
Concentration in Indo-Gangetic Plain (UP, Punjab, Haryana, Bihar, Rajasthan) due to alluvial aquifers
Distinction between open/dug wells (shallow, traditional) and tube wells (deep, mechanized) — different aquifer dependency
UPSC trap: tube well irrigation expanded massively post-Green Revolution due to electric pump subsidies, not just natural availability

concepts.name: Net Irrigated Area by Source: Comparative Share and Trends
key_dimensions: Ranking by share: Wells/tube wells > Canals > Tanks > Other sources — must-know order for MCQs
Declining share of tanks and canals over decades vs. rising dominance of groundwater-based irrigation
State-wise exceptions: canal irrigation still dominant in Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh's western districts
UPSC trap: 'gross irrigated area' vs. 'net irrigated area' — gross counts same land irrigated multiple times in a year

concepts.name: Groundwater Over-Exploitation and Dark/Grey/White Zone Classification
key_dimensions: Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) classification: White (safe), Grey (semi-critical), Dark/Red (over-exploited)
States with most over-exploited blocks: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan — directly linked to tube well-intensive Green Revolution agriculture
Legal and policy response: Model Groundwater (Sustainable Management) Bill, Atal Bhujal Yojana
UPSC trap: over-exploitation is NOT uniform — it is highly localized to specific blocks even within 'safe' states

concepts.name: Canal Irrigation and Waterlogging/Soil Salinization Problem
key_dimensions: Mechanism: excessive canal water seepage raises water table → waterlogging → capillary rise → salt deposition on surface (usar/reh soils)
Worst affected regions: Punjab, Haryana, western UP, Rajasthan canal commands (Indira Gandhi Canal area)
Distinction between waterlogging (physical problem) and salinization (chemical problem) — often co-occur but are different
UPSC trap: the Indira Gandhi Canal, despite bringing irrigation to Thar Desert, has ALSO caused waterlogging in parts of Ganganagar and Hanumangarh districts

concepts.name: Tank Irrigation: Community Management Systems and Revival Efforts
key_dimensions: Traditional community maintenance: Kudimaramath (Tamil Nadu) — participatory tank maintenance system revived by Tamil Nadu government
Role of Water User Associations (WUAs) and Panchayati Raj Institutions in tank restoration
Government schemes: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) — Har Khet Ko Pani component includes tank restoration
UPSC trap: Kudimaramath is a community practice, NOT a government scheme — the government 'revived' it, not created it

concepts.name: Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan Canal): Irrigation and Ecological Impact
key_dimensions: Largest irrigation canal project in India — originates from Harike Barrage (confluence of Sutlej and Beas), flows through Thar Desert
Dual impact: agricultural transformation of Ganganagar, Bikaner districts vs. ecological concerns (waterlogging, desertification disruption, loss of desert ecosystem)
Controversy: benefits concentrated in upper reaches; tail-end farmers face water scarcity — classic canal equity problem
UPSC trap: Indira Gandhi Canal is fed by Harike Barrage (Punjab), NOT a Rajasthan river — inter-state water dependency

concepts.name: Micro-Irrigation: Drip and Sprinkler Systems
key_dimensions: Drip irrigation: suited for horticultural crops, orchards, vegetables — saves 30-50% water vs. flood irrigation; concentrated in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh
Sprinkler irrigation: suited for uneven terrain, field crops like wheat and groundnut; common in Rajasthan, MP, UP
PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana — 'More Crop Per Drop' component specifically promotes micro-irrigation
UPSC trap: India has the LARGEST area under drip irrigation in the world — a frequently tested superlative

concepts.name: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY): Structure and Components
key_dimensions: Four components merged under PMKSY: AIBP (Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme), HKKP (Har Khet Ko Pani), MCPD (More Crop Per Drop), Watershed Development
AIBP focuses on completing long-pending major/medium irrigation projects — 'last mile connectivity'
District-level Irrigation Plans and State Irrigation Plans — decentralized planning approach
UPSC trap: PMKSY is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS), NOT a Central Sector Scheme — states share funding and implementation responsibility

concepts.name: Canal Irrigation: Command Area Development and Water Use Efficiency
key_dimensions: Command Area Development and Water Management Programme (CADWM) — aims to bridge gap between irrigation potential created and utilized
Field channels (field-to-farm water conveyance) as the 'last mile' problem in canal irrigation
Concept of Culturable Command Area (CCA) vs. Gross Command Area (GCA) — CCA is actually cultivable land within the command
UPSC trap: India has large gap between 'irrigation potential created' (IPC) and 'irrigation potential utilized' (IPU) — a governance failure, NOT a resource failure

concepts.name: Fluoride and Arsenic Contamination in Groundwater Irrigation
key_dimensions: Fluoride contamination: Rajasthan, Gujarat, AP, Telangana — causes fluorosis; linked to deep tube well extraction from fluoride-rich rock aquifers
Arsenic contamination: Bengal Basin, Bihar, Jharkhand, UP (Gangetic alluvial plains) — naturally occurring in shallow aquifers; worsened by over-extraction
Dual hazard: same groundwater used for both drinking and irrigation contaminates food chain (rice grown in arsenic-rich water)
UPSC trap: arsenic contamination is geogenic (natural) in origin in India, NOT primarily due to industrial pollution — unlike many other countries

concepts.name: Inter-State Water Disputes and Canal Irrigation Conflicts
key_dimensions: Constitutional provision: Article 262 — Parliament may adjudicate inter-state water disputes; bars Supreme Court jurisdiction
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 — framework for tribunals; major cases: Cauvery (Karnataka-Tamil Nadu), SYL Canal (Punjab-Haryana), Krishna, Godavari
SYL Canal dispute: Punjab's Termination of Agreements Act (2004) declared unconstitutional by SC — federalism vs. river water rights tension
UPSC trap: Article 262 does NOT permanently exclude Supreme Court — SC can still intervene on procedural/constitutional grounds, as seen in Cauvery case

concepts.name: Rain-Fed Agriculture vs. Irrigated Agriculture: Distribution and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: ~55% of India's net sown area is still rain-fed (unirrigated) — concentrated in eastern India, central India, and tribal regions
Rain-fed areas produce ~40% of food output and support majority of small/marginal farmers — equity dimension
National Rainfed Area Authority (NRAA) — set up to develop integrated strategies for rain-fed areas
UPSC trap: increasing irrigation coverage does NOT automatically improve rain-fed farmer income — soil health, market access, and crop diversification matter equally

concepts.name: Eastern India's Irrigation Paradox: Water-Rich but Under-Irrigated
key_dimensions: States like Bihar, Eastern UP, West Bengal, Odisha, Assam receive high rainfall AND have good groundwater, yet irrigation coverage is low
Reasons: fragmented land holdings, lack of rural electrification (historically), poor pump infrastructure, flooding-not-drought mindset, weak cooperative institutions
Policy response: Eastern India Green Revolution initiative — focus on rice intensification with improved irrigation in Bihar, WB, Eastern UP, Odisha
UPSC trap: the irrigation problem in Eastern India is NOT water scarcity but INSTITUTIONAL and INFRASTRUCTURAL failure — contrast with Punjab's over-exploitation

concepts.name: Lift Irrigation Schemes: Role and Regional Significance
key_dimensions: Lift irrigation: water pumped from rivers/reservoirs to higher elevation fields — important where gravity flow canals are not feasible
Significance in peninsular plateau states: Odisha (highest number of lift irrigation schemes), Maharashtra, AP — hard rock terrain, undulating topography
Energy dependency: lift irrigation is highly electricity-dependent — power subsidies to agriculture create fiscal stress on state discoms
UPSC trap: lift irrigation is classified separately from canal irrigation in official statistics even though it may use canal water — check source definitions in data questions

concepts.name: Watershed Development as a Supplementary Irrigation Strategy
key_dimensions: Watershed approach: in-situ rainwater harvesting through check dams, contour bunding, farm ponds — supplements irrigation in rain-fed areas
Key programmes: Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP) merged into PMKSY's watershed component; Mahatma Gandhi NREGS also funds watershed works
Success case: Hiware Bazar (Maharashtra) — participatory watershed development transforming drought-prone village into water-surplus area
UPSC trap: watershed development is NOT irrigation per se — it is water conservation and groundwater recharge; UPSC sometimes tests this definitional boundary

concepts.name: Irrigation Efficiency: Flood/Surface Irrigation vs. Pressurized Systems
key_dimensions: Water use efficiency by method: flood/furrow irrigation (~35-40%) < sprinkler (~70-75%) < drip (~90%) — important data for answers
India predominantly uses flood irrigation (especially for paddy and wheat) — huge scope for efficiency improvement
Economic vs. actual efficiency: even 'inefficient' flood irrigation may recharge groundwater, benefiting downstream users — social vs. private efficiency trade-off

UPSC trap: improving irrigation efficiency at farm level may REDUCE total basin-level water availability if return flows that previously recharged groundwater are eliminated — called the 'irrigation efficiency paradox'

concepts.name: State-wise Dominant Irrigation Source: Regional Patterns and Exceptions
key_dimensions: Canal dominant states: Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand, J&K (himalayan rivers), Andhra Pradesh (Krishna-Godavari delta)
Tank dominant states: Tamil Nadu, Andhra/Telangana (plateau regions), Karnataka — must-know for map-based questions
Well/tube well dominant states: Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra (for sugarcane), UP, Bihar
UPSC trap: Punjab uses BOTH canals AND tube wells heavily — it is the most intensively irrigated state overall but cannot be assigned a single dominant type without context
